name: fping - ICMP Host Discovery
description: Fast ICMP ping sweep to discover live hosts on a subnet. First recon step when entering an internal network — identifies all reachable hosts before port scanning. -a shows alive hosts only, -s prints stats, -g generates target range from CIDR, -q suppresses per-host output.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY FPING BEFORE NMAP ===
fping sends ICMP echo requests in parallel — much faster than sequential ping.
Use fping first to identify live hosts, then run nmap only against those.
Scanning all 254 hosts on a /24 with nmap -A takes much longer than:
  1. fping CIDR → alive.txt (seconds)
  2. nmap -iL alive.txt -A (minutes, only live hosts)

=== FLAGS ===
  -a    → only print alive hosts
  -s    → show statistics at end (total sent, received, lost)
  -g    → generate target range from CIDR (10.129.0.0/23)
  -q    → quiet (suppress per-target unreachable messages)

=== TYPICAL OUTPUT ===
  172.16.5.5
  172.16.5.25
  172.16.5.50
  172.16.5.225
  ...
  4 alive, 250 unreachable

Save to file: fping -asgq 172.16.5.0/23 | tee alive_hosts.txt

=== NMAP FOLLOWS ===
nmap -v -A -iL alive_hosts.txt -oN full_scan.txt
Targeted scan: find DC (port 389, 88, 636), workstations (port 445), web (80/443)

=== FIREWALL CONSIDERATIONS ===
ICMP may be blocked in some environments. Alternatives:
  nmap -sn <cidr>      → also tries ARP on local subnet
  crackmapexec smb <cidr> → SMB ping sweep (port 445)

defense.why_it_works: Live hosts answer ICMP/ARP; fping sends probes across a CIDR in parallel and reports responders, mapping the reachable attack surface fast.
defense.prerequisites: Network access to the internal subnet.
defense.impact: A live-host list for further enumeration and targeting.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1018] a burst of ICMP across the subnet from one source; internal host-discovery pattern.
defense.artifacts: ICMP probes across the range; the live-host list.
defense.prevention: Host firewalls dropping unsolicited ICMP; east-west monitoring for sweeps; segmentation.
defense.evasion: Use TCP/ARP discovery where ICMP is blocked/monitored; slow the sweep.
defense.misconfiguration: Active Directory's default read ACL allows any authenticated domain user to enumerate nearly the entire directory: all user accounts, groups, SPNs, computer objects, trust relationships, and many sensitive attributes. There is no built-in 'need to know' principle on LDAP reads. BloodHound, PowerView, and ldapsearch all exploit these open default ACLs to map attack paths.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# AD default permissions — authenticated users can read:
# All user objects: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, memberOf, servicePrincipalName
# All computer objects: DNS names, OS versions, operating system attributes
# All group memberships, GPOs, OU structure, domain trusts

# Verify with any low-priv account:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties *  # returns all users + attributes
Get-ADGroup -Filter * | Get-ADGroupMember  # all group memberships
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable AD Recycle Bin + Protected Users group
# 2. Audit and tighten ACLs on sensitive attributes:
#    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, adminCount, memberOf for privileged groups

# 3. Disable SMB null sessions + restrict LDAP anonymous binds (see smb/ldap cards)

# 4. Detect enumeration via volume:
# Sysmon Event 3 (network connection) from non-DC to DC on port 389/636
# Event 4661 — access to SAM objects (high-volume; baseline first)
# Microsoft Defender for Identity: 'Account Enumeration Reconnaissance' alert

# 5. Deploy Honey accounts/objects:
# Fake high-priv account (no real access) — any LDAP query for it = attacker
# BloodHound run from non-DC = detectable via DC LDAP traffic volume

# 6. Tiered administration: Tier 0 DCs, Tier 1 servers, Tier 2 workstations
#    Each tier can only query its own tier's objects

steps.label: Sweep the subnet for live hosts
